An advanced practice nurse is a registered or professional nurse who has acquired an expert knowledge base, advanced decision-making skills, and clinical competencies necessary for expanded practice. These characteristics are influenced by the context or country in which the nurse is credentialed to practice. A master’s degree is recommended as the entry-level qualification. (ICN 2017) 2. Age groups are subcategories of a population disaggregated by age. The recommended categories are: under 25, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, and 65 or older. (OECD 2017d) 3. Ambulatory care refers to personal health-care services provided by individuals or organizations on an outpatient basis. (Berman 2000) 4. An applicant is a person who applies for or requests entry into an educational program. (Oxford English Dictionary 2015; WHO 2006) 5. An associate professional nurse, or nursing associate professional (ISCO–2008 code 3221), typically works under the supervision of medical, nursing, or other health professionals to support the implementation of health care, treatment, and referral plans. (OECD 2017e) 6. Collaborative practice involves multiple health workers from different professional backgrounds working together to deliver high-quality, comprehensive services to patients, families, carers, and communities across various settings. This includes both clinical and non-clinical health-related work, such as diagnosis, treatment, surveillance, health communication, management, and sanitation engineering. (WHO 2010a) 7. Community health workers provide health education, referrals, follow-up, case management, basic preventive health care, and home visiting services to specific communities. They assist individuals and families in navigating health and social service systems. (International Labour Organization 2012) 8. The compensated absence rate is the number of workdays lost per health worker per year due to illness, excluding maternity leave. (OECD 2017d) 9. Compensation of employees refers to the total remuneration, in cash or kind, paid by an enterprise to an employee in return for work performed during the accounting period. This includes wages, salaries, social benefits, overtime payments, bonuses, allowances, and in-kind payments such as uniforms for medical staff. (OECD et al. 2011) 10. Continuing professional development (CPD) encompasses training beyond clinical updates, including research, scientific writing, professionalism, ethical practice, communication, leadership, management, team building, information technology, auditing, and attitudinal changes to improve patient services and research outcomes. CPD activities may include courses, lectures, training days, peer reviews, clinical audits, journal reading, conferences, and e-learning. CPD may be voluntary or mandatory, with verifiable and non-verifiable components. (WHO 2017b; WFME 2015) 11. Cost categories for health workforce expenditure include wages and salaries, social contributions, other employee-related costs, and self-employed professional remuneration. (OECD et al. 2011) 12. A domestically trained health worker is one who obtained their first qualification in the country where they are entitled to practice. (WHO 2010f) 13. The dropout rate refers to students from a cohort leaving health workforce education and training without completing it. (UNESCO 2009) 14. Dual practice involves a health worker engaging in multiple health-related practices at the same or different sites, which may include public-public, public-private, or private-private combinations. (Ferrinho et al.) 15. Education is the process by which societies deliberately transmit accumulated information, knowledge, understanding, attitudes, values, skills, competencies, and behaviors across generations. It involves communication designed to facilitate learning. (UNESCO 2012a) 16. Education levels are categorized as follows: early childhood education, primary education, lower secondary education, upper secondary education, post-secondary non-tertiary education, short-cycle tertiary education, bachelor’s or equivalent, master’s or equivalent, and doctorate or equivalent. (UNESCO 2012a) 17. Educational activities are deliberate actions involving communication intended to facilitate learning. Health and welfare activities are classified under the broad field code 09 in ISCED classification. (UNESCO 2014) 18. Employment is defined as persons of working age engaged in activities to produce goods or provide services for pay or profit during a short reference period. This includes those working at least one hour or temporarily absent from work due to arrangements like shift work or compensatory leave. (International Conference of Labour Statisticians 2013) 19. Enrollment refers to the number of new entrants in the first year of an educational program. (UNESCO 2009) 20. Facility or institution ownership types are classified as publicly owned, not-for-profit privately owned, or for-profit privately owned. Publicly owned facilities are controlled by governmental units or public corporations. Not-for-profit privately owned facilities are legal entities that do not generate income or profit for their founders. For-profit privately owned facilities are legal entities capable of generating profit for their owners. (European Communities et al. 2008) 21. Facility types include hospitals, residential long-term care facilities, providers of ambulatory health care, ancillary services (e.g., transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories), retailers (e.g., pharmacies), and providers of preventive care. (OECD et al. 2011) 22. Family medicine practitioners, classified under ISCO-08 code 2212, are generalist medical practitioners who provide person-centered, continuous, and comprehensive medical care to individuals and families in their communities. This group excludes resident medical officers, medical interns, and other generalist practitioners not engaged in general practice activities. 23. Field epidemiology training programs (FETPs) are health training programs involving field investigations to develop practical skills in epidemiological methods. Training levels include basic (local health staff, 3–5 months), intermediate (district/regional epidemiologists, 6–9 months), and advanced (national focus, 24 months). (WHO 2005b) 24. A foreign-born health worker is one born in a country other than the one where they perform health-related activities. (Wismar et al. 2011) 25. A foreign-trained health worker is a domestic health worker who obtained their qualification in another country and is entitled to practice in the receiving country. (OECD 2015b) 26. Full-time equivalent (FTE) employment is calculated as total hours worked divided by the average annual hours worked in a full-time job. Workers with full-time contracts are counted as 1 FTE, while part-time workers are measured based on their contracted hours relative to full-time hours. (OECD et al. 2016) 27. Gross domestic product (GDP) is the sum of final consumption expenditures, gross capital formation, and net exports. (OECD 2017c) 28. A gynecologist is a specialist medical practitioner (ISCO-08 code 2212) focused on functions and diseases specific to women and girls, particularly those affecting the reproductive system. (International Labour Organization 2012) 29. Health-care financing schemes are structural components of health-care financing systems, encompassing direct payments by households and third-party financing arrangements. These schemes govern participation, entitlement to services, and revenue pooling. Categories include government schemes, voluntary payment schemes, household out-of-pocket payments, and international financing schemes. (OECD et al. 2011) 30. A health information system supports decision-making through data generation, compilation, analysis, synthesis, and communication. It collects data from health and other sectors, ensures quality and relevance, and converts data into actionable information. (WHO 2010d) 31. Health professional mobility refers to the movement of health professionals across borders after graduation to deliver health-related services in the destination country, including during training periods. (Buchan et al. 2014) 32. A health workforce education and training institution is an accredited establishment providing education as its primary purpose, such as schools, colleges, universities, or training centers. These institutions may be public or private, for-profit or non-profit. (UNESCO 2012a) 33. Types of health workforce education and training institutions include public institutions (managed by public authorities) and private institutions (managed by private organizations or governing boards). Management, not funding, determines whether an institution is public or private. (UNESCO 2016)
